items.question: Is this going to need an engineer?
items.answer: Not for most of it. Builds are assembled visually, and the code escape hatch is there for the day you want it.

items.answer: Anything with an API that we maintain a connector for. Around eight thousand of them, and we keep them current so you do not have to.

items.question: What exactly is a build?
items.answer: One automated path: something Junction watches for, the steps that follow, and the rules wrapped around them.

items.question: How does a step get counted?
items.answer: A run is one execution of a build. Runs draw from a single shared balance across your account.

items.question: What kicks a build off?
items.answer: A new record, a clock, an inbound webhook, or a person pressing a button. Whichever fits the job.

items.question: Crew or Enterprise — how do I tell?

items.question: What if I pick the wrong tier?
items.answer: Move in either direction whenever you like. Upgrades prorate to the day, downgrades take effect at renewal.

items.answer: We do, and they are engineers first. Claim a session and you will get a plan, not a pitch.

items.answer: Crew gets priority email and chat during working hours. Enterprise gets a named engineer and a response window in writing.

defaultProps.body:
We are two founders who spent the last decade building and running small software businesses.

We know what support feels like when the team is still small. A bug report lands while you are shipping. A refund request arrives during a deploy. Someone asks the same onboarding question for the fifth time this week, and the person answering is the founder, the developer, or the one person who can actually fix it.

That kind of support is valuable. It keeps you close to your users. It shows you what is confusing, what is broken, and what to build next.

But most support tools were not designed for that. They were designed for large teams, complex workflows, sales calls, dashboards and long setup cycles.

So we built the tool we wished we had.

defaultProps.heading: Hey, but why “Halcyon”?
defaultProps.body:
Halcyon days are the calm ones — a stretch of still weather in the middle of winter, named after a bird that was supposed to nest on the water while the sea held its breath.

That is the bar we set for a support tool. Not louder, not busier. A steady, trustworthy way to carry a message from your customer to you, and your answer back to them.

It is a small thing to aim for, and a hard one to keep.

items.question: What is automated ops?
items.answer: Software that carries out an operational task end to end — reading the data, applying your policy, writing the result back — while recording who authorised it and why. It is not a chatbot bolted onto a queue.

items.question: How is this different from the automation we already have?
items.answer: Rule engines break the moment a case falls outside the rule. Quarry handles the judgement cases by escalating them with the full context attached, rather than dropping them into an exceptions report nobody reads.

items.question: Does our customer data leave our environment?
items.answer: No. Quarry holds pointers and executes against your systems using your credentials. Records stay in the tenancy they already live in.

items.question: Which industry systems can you connect to?
items.answer: Settlement and metering flows, the major billing platforms, your warehouse, and anything with a documented API. Connectors are configuration, not bespoke development.

items.question: How long does a first go-live take?
items.answer: One segment in about twelve weeks, including the evidence pack your compliance team signs off. Broader rollout follows segment by segment.

items.question: How do you handle model changes?
items.answer: Models are pinned per workflow and versioned with the policy that invoked them. A change is a deliberate, reviewable event, never a silent upgrade.
